kid.question: Toward what does Jonah say he will look again?

options.text: Nineveh's great wall
Joppa's busy harbor
God's holy temple
Tarshish's distant shore

kid.explanation: Even after saying he is cast out of God's sight, Jonah resolves to look again toward His holy temple.

kid.question: What does Jonah promise to offer with his sacrifice?

options.text: A voice of thanksgiving
A promise of fasting
A gift of firstfruits
A plea for guidance

kid.explanation: Jonah promises sacrifice with thanksgiving and payment of his vows, declaring salvation to be the Lord's.

kid.question: What happens when the Lord speaks to the fish?

options.text: Jonah is carried back to his ship
Jonah is taken into Nineveh's river
Jonah is shown a distant island
Jonah is released onto dry land

kid.explanation: At the Lord's word, the fish vomits Jonah onto dry land.

kid.question: What does Jonah do when the Lord sends him a second time?

options.text: Waits near the harbor
Goes to Nineveh
Sails toward Tarshish
Returns to his village

kid.explanation: This time Jonah arises and goes to Nineveh according to the Lord's word.

kid.question: How long does Jonah say it will be before Nineveh is overthrown?

options.text: Seven days
Thirty days
Seventy days
Forty days

kid.explanation: Jonah announces that Nineveh will be overthrown in forty days.

kid.question: What does Nineveh's king do after hearing the message?

options.text: Calls his army and guards the gates
Sends his servants to offer silver
Leaves his throne and sits in ashes
Puts on his crown and addresses Jonah

kid.explanation: The king rises from his throne, removes his robe, covers himself with sackcloth, and sits in ashes.

kid.question: Which change does the king name in his decree?

options.text: Turn away from evil and violence
Give back land taken from neighbors
Free the captives held in prison
Replace the judges accused of taking bribes

kid.explanation: The decree calls for crying to God and each person turning from evil ways and violence.

kid.question: How does Jonah feel when Nineveh is spared?

options.text: Greatly relieved
Very angry
Quietly curious
Deeply confused

kid.explanation: God does not carry out the announced destruction, and Jonah is exceedingly displeased and angry.

kid.question: Why is Jonah glad about the plant?

options.text: It bears fruit for his meal
It marks the path to the city
It shelters his water jar
It gives shade over his head

kid.explanation: God prepares the gourd to shade Jonah and deliver him from grief, and Jonah is exceedingly glad of it.

kid.question: Who else is mentioned in God's final question about Nineveh?

options.text: The many cattle
The foreign soldiers
The visiting merchants
The royal musicians

kid.explanation: Along with the city's many people, the Lord explicitly mentions 'also much cattle.'

high-school.question: What contrast shapes Jonah's prayer about the depths?

options.text: He describes confinement yet credits the sailors with guiding his rescue
He describes confinement yet credits the Lord with bringing up his life
He describes a voyage yet credits Nineveh's king with opening its harbor
He describes a voyage yet credits the captain with providing a second ship

high-school.explanation: Waves, depths, weeds, and the earth's bars surround him, yet he says the Lord has brought his life up from corruption.

high-school.question: How does Jonah 2:9 frame his promised future worship?

options.text: A pilgrimage and a rebuilt altar express his gratitude for divine rescue
A fast and an offering of grain precede his return to dry land
Renewed temple service and a public feast fulfill his previously made vows
Thankful sacrifice and paid vows accompany his confession of the Lord's salvation

high-school.explanation: Jonah promises thankful sacrifice and fulfillment of vows, then declares that salvation belongs to the Lord.

high-school.question: What is Jonah told about the content of his second mission?

options.text: Preach the message the Lord gives him
Report the message the sailors gave him
Choose the message the king will accept
Repeat the message the nobles have prepared

high-school.explanation: The Lord tells Jonah to preach what He bids him; Jonah then announces Nineveh's overthrow in forty days.

high-school.question: How does the account show the breadth of Nineveh's response?

options.text: Greatest and least respond, with the king joining in abasement
Priests respond first, with the royal household continuing its feast
Travelers respond first, with the city's residents waiting for a second sign
Soldiers and merchants respond, with the nobles sending them outside the walls

high-school.explanation: Belief, fasting, and sackcloth extend from greatest to least, followed by the king leaving his throne for sackcloth and ashes.

high-school.question: What hope does the king voice after calling for change?

options.text: God may accept tribute in place of the nation's required fast
God may send a second prophet to explain the forty days
God may turn from fierce anger so they do not perish
God may appoint Jonah as judge over the repentant city

high-school.explanation: The decree calls for changed conduct and asks, 'Who can tell' whether God will relent so they do not perish.

high-school.question: What does God see when deciding not to carry out the announced destruction?

options.text: Their wealth, brought before the royal throne
Their works, turning from their evil way
Their walls, repaired after the public gathering
Their offerings, measured by the city's temple priests

high-school.explanation: The text specifically identifies their works and turning from evil as what God sees.

high-school.question: What reason does Jonah give for his earlier flight?

options.text: He thought the Lord had already destroyed the city
He knew the sailors would carry the warning for him
He thought the king had forbidden entry to prophets
He knew the Lord was merciful and might relent

high-school.explanation: Jonah explains his flight by naming the Lord's grace, mercy, slowness to anger, kindness, and relenting.

high-school.question: How does the Lord first respond to Jonah's anger?

options.text: He asks whether Jonah is ready to return home
He asks whether Jonah has paid his promised vows
He asks whether Jonah is right to be angry
He asks whether Jonah will wait another forty days

high-school.explanation: After Jonah asks to die, the Lord responds with a question about whether his anger is right.

high-school.question: What sequence turns Jonah's pleasure into renewed distress?

options.text: A storm floods the shelter, then hail and rain drive him away
A worm withers the plant, then wind and sun overwhelm him
A fire burns the shelter, then smoke and thirst exhaust him
A beast eats the plant, then hunger and darkness overcome him

high-school.explanation: The Lord prepares the plant, a worm attacks it, and then a vehement east wind and the sun leave Jonah faint.

high-school.question: How does the final comparison challenge Jonah's priorities?

options.text: His pity for a plant is set beside God's concern for a city
His pity for a plant is set beside the sailors' concern for their cargo
His desire for a shelter is set beside the king's desire for a new palace
His desire for a shelter is set beside the farmers' desire for another harvest

high-school.explanation: Jonah pities a plant he did not grow; the Lord asks whether He should spare Nineveh's many people and cattle.

expert.question: How do the temple references in Jonah's prayer sustain its movement from distress to hope?

options.text: He resolves to rebuild it and describes the king supplying materials for it
He recalls leaving it and describes the sailors carrying his offering there
He recalls serving in it and describes the priests sending a message from it
He resolves to look toward it and describes his prayer reaching God there

expert.explanation: Looking again toward the holy temple is followed by remembrance of the Lord and prayer entering His holy temple.

expert.question: What contrast does Jonah 2:8-9 draw around mercy and salvation?

options.text: Those delaying offerings forfeit mercy; Jonah promises fasting before paying his vows
Those pursuing vanities forsake mercy; Jonah promises thankful sacrifice and paid vows
Those breaking vows forfeit rescue; Jonah promises new offerings at the temple
Those fleeing Nineveh lose mercy; Jonah promises to accept the city's commission

expert.explanation: Those observing lying vanities forsake their mercy, while Jonah promises thankful worship and declares salvation to be of the Lord.

expert.question: What does the transition from Jonah 2:10 to 3:1-3 join together?

options.text: Release onto land is followed by renewed commission and obedience
Release onto land is followed by public reward and royal appointment
A renewed storm is followed by renewed commission and obedience
A renewed storm is followed by public reward and royal appointment

expert.explanation: The fish releases Jonah at the Lord's word; the word then comes a second time, and Jonah goes as directed.

expert.question: How does the narrative distinguish Nineveh's external signs from its decisive change?

options.text: Fasting and sackcloth replace the turning from evil that God had requested
Fasting and sackcloth await Jonah's return before the king can change conduct
Fasting and sackcloth accompany the turning from evil that God sees
Fasting and sackcloth secure a new warning before God examines their conduct

expert.explanation: The public acts include fasting, sackcloth, and ashes; the decree calls for changed conduct, and God sees that they turn from evil.

expert.question: What links the king's uncertainty in verse 9 with the narrator's account in verse 10?

options.text: A hoped-for delay becomes a narrated demand for another public sacrifice
A promised relenting becomes a narrated reward for completing forty days
A hoped-for relenting becomes a narrated response to changed works
A promised delay becomes a narrated transfer of the city to foreign rule

expert.explanation: The king asks who can tell whether God will turn; the narrator then says God sees their changed works and does not do the threatened evil.

expert.question: What tension does Jonah's explanation of his flight reveal?

options.text: Knowledge of God's merciful character coexists with anger at its exercise
Fear of punishment for Nineveh coexists with reluctance to deliver its warning
Confidence in Nineveh's destruction coexists with refusal to announce a timetable
Desire to protect Israel coexists with hope that Nineveh will reject the warning

expert.explanation: Jonah is angry when the city is spared and says he fled because he knew God's gracious and merciful character.

expert.question: Which question does the Lord repeat in Jonah 4, applying it later to the gourd?

options.text: Whether Jonah remembers his vows to God
Whether Jonah does well to be angry
Whether Jonah will return to the city
Whether Jonah has shown mercy to others

expert.explanation: The Lord asks whether Jonah does well to be angry, and later asks the same concerning the gourd; Jonah defends his anger unto death.

expert.question: How do the prepared plant, worm, and wind function together?

options.text: The Lord removes relief and then restores it before renewing Jonah's commission
The Lord gives relief and then removes it before renewing Jonah's commission
The Lord removes relief and then restores it before questioning Jonah's pity
The Lord gives relief and then removes it before questioning Jonah's pity

expert.explanation: The Lord provides shade, the worm destroys it, and wind and sun deepen distress, setting up the comparison between Jonah's pity and God's.

expert.question: What asymmetry grounds the final plant-and-city comparison?

options.text: Jonah pities a plant he had grown; God asks about rebuilding a temple
Jonah pities a plant he did not grow; God asks about sparing a city
Jonah pities a plant he did not grow; God asks about rebuilding a temple
Jonah pities a plant he had grown; God asks about sparing a city

expert.explanation: The Lord names Jonah's lack of labor and the plant's brief life before asking about sparing Nineveh, with its many people and cattle.

expert.question: How does the book's final form place a demand on the reader?

options.text: It ends with God's question about Nineveh, followed by Jonah's promise to return
It ends with God's question about Nineveh, followed by the city's public thanksgiving
It ends with God's question about Nineveh, without recording Jonah's reply
It ends with God's declaration of mercy, followed by Jonah's renewed protest

expert.explanation: The last words are the Lord's question about Nineveh's people and cattle; the text records no subsequent answer from Jonah.
